package_info.package_manager: N/A (malware distributed via phishing, not a package manager)
package_info.why_malicious: IcedID is a banking trojan distributed via phishing attacks and exploits, designed to gain unauthorized access to internal networks, perform credential theft, and enable cyberespionage. It is used by threat actors to compromise government entities and exfiltrate sensitive data.

execution_context.trigger: runtime (after phishing document execution or exploit)
execution_context.file_location: dropped executable or macro within malicious document

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Process injection code that injects malicious payload into explorer.exe or other legitimate processes to evade detection and maintain persistence.
malicious_snippets.code_language: C/C++ (compiled binary, typical for IcedID payloads)
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code injects a malicious payload into a legitimate system process (e.g., explorer.exe), allowing the malware to operate under the guise of a trusted process, evade security controls, and establish persistence.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Process injection is a common technique used by malware to hide its presence and bypass endpoint security solutions.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software does not inject code into unrelated system processes without user consent or clear operational need.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some security tools or debuggers may inject code for monitoring or debugging purposes, but this is rare and typically well-documented.
key_indicators: Unusual process injection into explorer.exe or other system processes
Execution of code from memory regions not associated with the original process

execution_context.file_location: malware main module or injected code

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: HTTP(S) POST requests to command-and-control (C2) servers, exfiltrating stolen credentials and system information.
malicious_snippets.code_language: C/C++ (networking code within the malware binary)
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code collects credentials and system information, then sends this data via HTTP(S) POST requests to remote command-and-control servers controlled by the attacker.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Unsolicited outbound network connections to untrusted domains, especially with sensitive data, are a hallmark of credential-stealing malware.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal applications do not exfiltrate credentials or system information to external servers without user consent.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some enterprise software may send telemetry, but not credentials or sensitive data, and only to trusted domains.
key_indicators: Outbound HTTP(S) POST requests to suspicious or unrecognized domains
Transmission of credential or system data in network payloads

attack_chain.action: Victim receives phishing email or is targeted via Zimbra exploit, leading to execution of a malicious document or payload.
Malicious payload executes and injects code into legitimate system processes to evade detection and establish persistence.
attack_chain.leads_to: Stealthy operation and further malicious activity

attack_chain.action: Malware collects credentials and system information from the infected host.
Stolen data is exfiltrated to attacker-controlled command-and-control servers.
attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker gains access to internal networks and can perform further cyberespionage

behavioral_signatures: Process injection into explorer.exe or other system processes
Unusual outbound HTTP(S) POST requests following document execution
Credential or system information collection immediately after infection
file_indicators: Malicious Office documents with embedded macros
Dropped executables in temporary or user profile directories
Unusual DLLs or binaries loaded into system processes
network_indicators: Outbound connections to known IcedID C2 infrastructure
HTTP(S) POST requests with credential data to untrusted domains
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for process injection events, especially into explorer.exe or other system processes, following the execution of Office documents or email attachments. Inspect outbound network traffic for HTTP(S) POST requests to suspicious domains, particularly those containing credential or system data. Use endpoint protection solutions capable of detecting banking trojans and credential theft behaviors.
